title: Town of Turtle votes to recall chairperson - WMTV 15 NEWS
text: ROCK COUNTY, Wis. (WMTV) - The Town of Turtle has voted to recall its chairperson. With 634 votes cast at the Turtle Town Hall, challenger Donna Redner won the race to oust incumbent Roger Anclam on Tuesday night. Redner earned 400 votes, earning 63.09% of the vote. Anclam received 232 votes, earning 26.59% of the vote. According to Rockford News First, a Gray Media sister station of WMTV, the recall effort was grown from several disputes in the town, including plans surrounding the Lathers Road Bridge and a debate over a potential data center. title: Madison police chief wants officers to think critically about use of force - WPR
text: Madison Police Chief John Patterson says his city is long overdue for adopting police body cameras. “It’s such a relief, I have to say, to finally be moving towards this technology,” Patterson told WPR’s “Wisconsin Today.” “And frankly, it’s a technology that almost the entire rest of the state has deployed within their communities.” For more than a decade, the city has been divided over whether or not to equip its officers with cameras, with some community activists worried about how the footage might be used. But after a Madison police officer fatally shot Corey Ruiz on July 22 , a new call for cameras emerged. At the end of September, the city announced that thanks to a grant from the Madison Community Foundation, all officers will have them by the end of 2027.  WPR’s “Wisconsin Today” newsletter keeps you connected to the state you love without feeling overwhelmed. No paywall. No agenda. No corporate filter. The police department is also promising to better scrutinize how officers are using force with the creation of the Service Excellence and Outreach Section.  Patterson told WPR’s “ Wisconsin Today ” that the effort to better evaluate officers’ performance isn’t directly a result of the Ruiz killing. “We need to be more proactive in the law enforcement field and not just acknowledge the data that’s at our fingertips, but use it in a way that will be more responsive to our community and improve as we can,” he said. Patterson spoke to “Wisconsin Today” about the changes in the works for the department. The following has been edited for clarity and brevity. Kate Archer Kent: How do you envision this Service Excellence and Outreach Section operating?  John Patterson: Nothing can impact negatively the trust that you have in your community more than any instance, frankly, of use of force. Right now, I could tell you how many instances of use of force have occurred in the downtown district, for example, in Madison this last month. I don’t have at my fingertips all of the decision points that went into every specific instance where force was used. We need to dedicate resources that will allow us to dissect each incident and, in a proactive and professional development way, walk our staff through each of their decision points, get them to think critically, and really embrace the core value that we have of continuous improvement, and try to see if there aren’t better ways to approach the same situations. KAK: How did the Madison Police Department evaluate its officers when they used deadly force, and then what will change?  JP: We fortunately don’t have frequent occurrences of the use of deadly force, but we do look at all use of force on a biweekly basis. I’m provided summaries of each specific incident, and then each month, I’m given a further breakdown of where they’re occurring within our workforce, what trends we’re seeing in our workforce demographics, and then across districts as well. That’s an opportunity to bring the community closer to the table and have those same discussions with us, help us look at instances in their entirety, but also what commonalities are we seeing, or what stark differences we may be seeing from one district to another, for example, or from one shift to another. KAK: What are some benchmarks for progress? What are you aiming toward?  JP: Right now we can very easily tell which officers are using force more than others. That’s not saying that they’re necessarily doing anything wrong, but we should look at all the other factors at our fingertips as well, like the types of calls that they may be disproportionately responding to than others, what differences might exist in the district that they’re serving? What differences might exist within their shift, and if there are other supportive measures like training that we can offer, that’s what we’re hoping to achieve. … We should never just look at a specific outcome and walk away from it, even if it was a good outcome. There are always things that we can learn from, do differently, and improve upon. KAK: The department’s use of force policy says that officers are obligated to intervene when they witness another officer using excessive force. How challenging is it for an officer to rein in a fellow officer? JP: In some environments, it could be very challenging. What we try to do is foster an environment where psychological safety exists. Any police officer, any employee, should feel very comfortable making mistakes, and understanding that they can learn from them. They also must be very comfortable asking questions of their supervisors, asking questions when decisions are made, and not live in a work environment where they’re living in fear of admonishment or retribution. So really, from the minute they enter our doors, we try to foster this concept of psychological safety because if I don’t feel comfortable working in an environment where I might be able to learn from a mistake or ask questions of a supervisor without retribution, how could I possibly be expected to then intervene when I’m seeing something wrong? Trying to create that culture of learning and fostering that psychological safety is critically important in this profession.  KAK: But time in those moments is also very critical. So, you know, quoting from the policy, an officer observing the use of excessive force shall notify an uninvolved supervisor as soon as practicable. But what if it’s too late? What if the permanent harm has been done? JP : That’s a fantastic question and that’s part of what we’re also hoping to really get us thinking critically about. Twenty-five years ago, when I was a new officer, I had just joined the SWAT team. We were evaluated on how quickly we could execute a search warrant. For example, I remember my supervisor literally with a stopwatch, ensuring that we could get through a door and into our area within seven to 10 seconds. And now our SWAT team has gone completely on the other end of the spectrum, and they’re going out of their way to maximize time and space so that decisions are not becoming compressed, and so that options are not limited. That’s something that we really have to focus on, breaking down our decisions in all of the different points. … Hopefully maximizing that time and space will create even greater opportunity, not just for de-escalation, but for intervention if that’s what needs to occur.

title: Republican Sen. Patrick Testin weighs Wisconsin Senate battle
text: MADISON, Wis. — Republican Sen. Patrick Testin during an interview with "For the Record" weighed in as Wisconsin Republicans work to protect their state Senate majority in an election that could reshape control of state government. Democrats have their first opportunity in 16 years to win a governing trifecta — control of the governor’s office, state Senate and state Assembly. To take the Senate majority, Democrats must flip two seats. Four races have emerged as key contests: the 17th Senate District in southwestern Wisconsin, the 31st Senate District in the Eau Claire area, the 5th Senate District in Milwaukee’s suburbs and the 21st Senate District south of Milwaukee. The Senate is competitive in part because of Wisconsin’s new legislative maps, which Gov. Tony Evers signed into law in 2024. State senators serve staggered four-year terms, meaning not every Senate district was on the ballot under the new boundaries in 2024. The 2026 election will be the first in which the full effect of the redistricting is felt across the Senate seats up for election. Republicans are seeking to maintain their current majority in the chamber. ​COPYRIGHT 2026 BY CHANNEL 3000. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. title: Madison Common Council fires Interim Independent Police Monitor, after job performance controversy - WMTV 15 NEWS
text: MADISON, Wis. (WMTV) - The Madison Common Council voted 14-6 Wednesday morning to terminate Interim Independent Police Monitor Aeiramique Glass, effective immediately. This is how every common council member voted: Aye No The meeting lasted over 12 hours, starting at 6:30 p.m. Tuesday. The Common Council adjourned the meeting just before 6:42 a.m. Wednesday. The vote on Item 79 followed weeks of controversy over her job performance outlined in an Oct. 2 employment review from the City Attorney’s office. That review, requested by alders including Council President Sabrina Madison, states Glass, hired Dec. 8, 2025, primarily to lead the search for a permanent monitor, had made no meaningful progress after nearly 10 months, with no approved job description, posting or interviews. It also cited a missed July 17 budget deadline, disputes over contracting authority, strained relationships with Madison police, the Dane County DA and state DOJ, and an open outside investigation into complaints about Glass’s own conduct. Tensions rose significantly following the July police shooting death of Corey Ruiz. The review notes a Dane County Circuit Court granted a protective order for a Madison officer against Glass based on on-the-job actions. The Police Civilian Oversight Board says the City Attorney document is not the official performance evaluation, noting it completed its own internal survey. Glass has disputed the review’s legitimacy in a Facebook livestream. Tuesday morning, Common Council President Sabrina Madison posted framing the decision around effective oversight, writing race is being “weaponized when accusations of racism are used to shut down debate” over Glass, and fear of being labeled racist should not stop honest conversation on performance. She wrote the question is not whether oversight matters, but whether Glass is moving the city toward it. More than 140 people registered to speak. Public comment was expected to take hours, with a majority of speakers holding “Justice for Corey Ruiz” signs. Despite the missed deadline, funding for the office remains in active debate. A speaker during the executive budget hearing urged the council to increase funding for the OIM, echoing the Oversight Board’s call to fund civilian oversight at 1% of the Madison Police Department’s budget. The office requested about $781,158 for 2027. The city recommended flat, cost-to-continue funding. Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway said it was the only agency that submitted no 2% reduction and did not meet budget deadlines. The resolution does not eliminate the Office of the Independent Monitor. The Council Chief of Staff will temporarily supervise OIM staff until a permanent monitor is hired, and will work with Finance to engage the National Association of Civilian Oversight of Law Enforcement (NACOLE) on next steps. Glass’s interim appointment had run through March 31, 2027. Click here to download the WMTV15 News app or our WMTV15 First Alert weather app. Copyright 2026 WMTV. All rights reserved.

title: Milwaukee tests election equipment ahead of Election Day - Spectrum News
text: MILWAUKEE — Milwaukee election officials are preparing for what is expected to be a busy Election Day on Nov. 3, holding a public test of ballot-counting equipment Saturday as the city works to maintain trust in the process. Public testing of election equipment is standard procedure before elections in Wisconsin. Milwaukee Election Commission Director Paulina Gutierrez showed the machines that will count ballots on Election Day as members of the public watched the process. “We may see jams early, but then as it starts processing those thousands and thousands of ballots, it gets in the swing of things,” Gutierrez said. Among those attending the test were Ben Ginsberg and Bob Bauer, co-chairs of a national organization called Pillars of the Community. “Pillars of the Community is very active in seven states, they’re contentious battleground states where election-related issues have been raised before,” Bauer said. Ginsberg said the group uses experience from both sides of the political spectrum to help build public confidence in elections. “States have different ways of running their elections, and so as we go around the country we get to see those different ways,” Ginsberg said. “Truth is, all of them are reliable.” Both Ginsberg and Bauer said they came away from Saturday’s test without doubts that the election will run smoothly in Milwaukee. Gutierrez said the city is also looking for additional poll workers to help on Election Day. “People sometimes cancel at the last minute, it’s always really hard, it’s a long day, some people just want to do partial shifts,” Gutierrez said. “We want that buffer so in the event it’s busy we’ve got enough staff.” The preparations come as Milwaukee faces added attention after three election-related issues since 2024, including during the August primary. Gutierrez said the people involved in administering the election are focused on making sure ballots are counted accurately and efficiently. “The poll workers, the observers, attorneys, chief inspectors, absentee ballot board of canvassers, everybody is watching this process to ensure that it is safe, secure and fair,” she said.

title: Home repair costs jump 76% in a decade
text: Home improvement and repair costs have escalated over the last decade, adding to the strain of tight budgets for Americans, a new analysis finds. The median cost of a home improvement project has risen 76.1% from 2015 to 2025, from $1,200 to an inflation-adjusted $2,113, according to a LendingTree analysis. "Home improvement costs are increasing so much in part because the price of most anything is going up. The cost of labor and building is likely playing a big role," Matt Schulz, LendingTree chief consumer finance analyst, told USA Today. On Oct. 7, a roofer removes shingles from a house in New Bedford, Massachusetts, before putting on a new roof. Homeowners are staying in their homes longer rather than moving, and with that come repairs and upgrades, said Schulz. "Plenty of families feel stuck because they have a house that doesn’t meet their current needs but a mortgage rate that is far lower than what they’d get today. They simply can’t bring themselves to trade their 3% rate for a 7% rate, so they’re staying put. That isn’t likely to change anytime soon, unfortunately," he said. Routine maintenance on owner-occupied homes is an estimated $1,433 a year on average, but that amount rises to $1,706 annually for homes built before 1940. New properties are the cheapest to maintain, with costs falling to three figures for homes built in 2015 and later, LendingTree said. Houses built from 2022 to 2023 cost $173 on average to maintain. Sixty-four percent of the projects analyzed were completed by a professional, with the median project costing an estimated $4,103. That's compared to $845 spent on a DIY project. LendingTree analyzed U.S. Census Bureau American Housing Survey and U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) data for its analysis. Nearly 6 in 10 owner-occupied homes, or 51.6 million of the nation's 86.9 million owner-occupied properties, underwent some type of improvement during the research's two-year lookback window. There were 139.9 million individual projects, or an average of 2.7 projects per improved home. But the most common project wasn't a big renovation. The most common single project category was a combined group covering water heaters, dishwashers and garbage disposals, with homeowners adding or replacing appliances in 11.7% of all projects tracked. The median cost was $845. Schulz said it doesn't surprise him that maintenance and repairs account for the biggest projects. "Home improvements may be bigger and flashier, but ongoing maintenance and repairs are more common. Most any homeowner can tell you that they just never seem to stop," he said. "They might only cost a few hundred dollars rather than the several thousand dollars people may spend on larger renovations, but they happen so regularly that it can add up to a major financial burden for families." Cash savings covered 75.7% of home-improvement projects, with only 6.3% of projects being paid with credit cards and 3.9% using homeowners insurance settlements, according to the analysis. Cash tends to fund the smaller home-improvement jobs, with the median cash-funded project costing an estimated $1,902. Homeowners turned to other sources for more expensive projects, with home equity loans being used for median projects of $7,924 and insurance settlements funding median projects costing $9,963.

title: Upcoming midterm election sees new opportunities for student representation - The Badger Herald
text: As the Nov. 3 midterm election approaches, news has been dominated by political coverage of candidates running for political offices and positions across Wisconsin. With combined advertising and campaign spending totaling over $80 million, Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Crowley and Republican gubernatorial candidate Tom Tiffany spent substantial amounts criticizing each other to reach voters statewide, according to WisPolitics . Many political offices and candidates have received little or no media attention, raising concerns about straight ticket party-affiliated voting or low voter turnout, an issue often seen during midterm elections. Along with the gubernatorial race, offices such as Lieutenant Governor, Attorney General, Secretary of State, State Treasurer, District 2 of the U.S. House, District 76 or 77 of the Wisconsin State Assembly and Dane County-specific positions are all on the ballot for Madison voters . Additionally, three constitutional amendments will be on the ballot that would limit the governor’s partial veto to create or limit any tax or fee, prevent religious gatherings from being restricted during emergencies and prohibit discrimination within state and local governments as well as public education institutions . If passed, these GOP-led referendums would amend the Wisconsin State Constitution without the governor’s approval, according to League of Women Voters of Dane County member Andrea Kaminski. “It’s really important for people to understand the amendments, what they’re [politicians] trying to do with them, and often they’re developed by politicians or the party that doesn’t have the governor’s office because they don’t want their proposal to get vetoed,” Kaminski said. Kaminski said she acknowledges that the amendments’ language may be confusing and may do the opposite of what it proposes, which can confuse voters, and she urges voters to seek out what the amendments truly mean. To help voters learn more about local races and elections, voter guides such as Vote411.org , created by LWV, can provide information on specific ballot topics like constitutional amendments, according to Kaminski. Vote411.org also provides information about candidates and their positions on local and controversial issues such as data centers, reproductive health, LGBTQ+ issues, abortion and educational funding, according to Kaminski. Inflation and broader economic development and policy are most likely to drive voters to the polls for federal elections rather than state and local elections, according to Kaminski. “When you’re voting for the state legislature, as opposed to the federal level, you’re talking about issues that are closer to our everyday lives, and they can have an immediate effect,” Kaminski said. “It’s really important to understand those and make your choice on them.” As local and midterm elections receive less voter turnout than federal elections, concerns of equal and accurate representation arise, as the demographic of those who vote in midterm elections tends to be older, more educated and of higher socioeconomic status, according to University of Wisconsin political science Professor Barry Burden . “This means that young people are significantly underrepresented in midterm elections as they vote at much lower rates,” Burden said. “The electorate is just skewed towards older and higher-resource voters in midterms.” With little connection to their communities and little party affiliation, younger people are often less knowledgeable or engaged in midterm and local elections than in presidential races, according to Burden. In the 2022 midterm election, people 65 years or older made up nearly a third of the electorate at 30.4% of voters but only 23.8% of the citizen voting-age population, according to the U.S. Census Bureau . Younger people ages 18 to 29 accounted for 11.7% of voters despite being 19.6% of the citizen voting-age population, showing how younger people had less voter turnout despite being a part of a large voting-eligible population, according to the U.S. Census Bureau. While there is equal access to information about candidates and races, younger voters are less knowledgeable about what is occurring in Congress, less familiar with candidate names on the ballot and overall less familiar with the responsibilities that offices play, according to Burden. Because ballots lack specific information on candidates, voters may default to straight-party voting based on party affiliation and partisanship, which can further skew the electorate and reduce representation accuracy, according to Burden. However, Burden said younger voters, especially students, could receive more representation by increasing voter registration and encouraging voters to head to the polls. “Wisconsin elections tend to be close at the statewide level, and thousands of students at UW-Madison could easily make up the difference,” Burden said. “In the last few governors’ races, the margin has been close enough that students could have made the difference.” Resources such as PBS Wisconsin, Wisconsin Public Radio, WisconsinVote.org and Vote411.org can provide necessary information on candidate profiles and voting information, according to Burden.

title: Trans Election Night Guide: The Biggest Elections To Watch For Trans People In 2026 - Erin In The Morning
text: Erin Reed Oct 28, 2026 126 12 20 Share Photo by Darren Halstead on Unsplash Erin In The Morning is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a subscriber. Election night is coming, and the results on Nov. 3 could be enormously consequential for transgender people across the United States. As the federal government has become openly hostile toward trans and queer people and Republican-controlled statehouses continue to pass a slew of anti-trans legislation, Democrats appear poised to make significant gains, perhaps even approaching a wave election. Races from the state legislative level all the way up to control of Congress will draw heavy attention from anyone hoping for Democratic victories, and transgender people are likely to be among those most affected by the results. Every year at Erin In The Morning, we watch the elections closely. We report on the results as they come in on election night ( subscribe and watch for our live chat if you have not already), and in the days that follow, we untangle what they mean. Before election night, we also put out guides so that you know which races will matter most for whatever narrative emerges about transgender people the day after. So here are the races we are watching on election night: Democratic control of the Senate is important for transgender people for so many reasons. Democrats in the driver’s seat in the Senate means a second chamber that can help keep anti-transgender riders out of must-pass legislation, and should Democrats choose to limit the Trump administration’s ability to target transgender people through such bills, control of the Senate would be enormously consequential. The Senate is also responsible for confirming any Supreme Court justices, and Democratic control of the chamber insulates us from further backsliding there. Likewise, many of these races have seen heavy ad spending around transgender people, sometimes with even the Democrat pushing anti-transgender ads, and whether those candidates win or lose will become part of the narrative moving forward. Here are the most important Senate races we are watching that have featured transgender issues: Michigan: Abdul El-Sayed (D) vs. Mike Rogers (R). This race is probably one of the most important races in the country for transgender people. Should El-Sayed win, it will show that a Democrat running on unequivocal support for transgender people in a relatively purple state can win. A win by El-Sayed dampens any narrative that transgender people must be thrown under the bus for a Democratic victory. Minnesota: Peggy Flanagan (D) vs. Michele Tafoya (R). This is a clean test of whether or not a Democrat needs to embrace anti-transgender policy to win a contested election. Flanagan wore a “protect trans kids” T-shirt to Walz’s signing of an executive order protecting gender-affirming care. Tafoya has been vehemently anti-transgender . Maine: Susan Collins (R) vs. Troy Jackson (D). This race has been one of the focal races for Elon Musk’s America PAC, which has poured $100 million into races across the country, many of which feature ads targeting transgender people . title: Tom Tiffany: What to know about the Republican running for governor
text: MADISON, Wis. — With one week until Election Day, U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany is campaigning across Wisconsin. “We are covering every corner of the state of Wisconsin. I'm going to be the governor for all 72 counties,” Tiffany said. “I'm a lifelong resident, raised our family here. My wife and I owned and operated our own business. I'm a regular Wisconsin guy." title: Big donors shape spending in Wisconsin’s 2026 legislative, gubernatorial elections - The Badger Herald
text: Republican groups are outraising and outspending Democratic groups in the fight for control of the Wisconsin Legislature, with financial gaps in both the State Senate and Assembly. The donations are helping fund Republican campaign committees’ efforts to elect candidates and maintain control of the Wisconsin Senate and Assembly as they have for roughly 15 years, while the Democrats are pushing to flip both chambers in the Nov. 3 elections. The financial gap is most prominent in the Assembly, where the Republican Assembly Campaign Committee raised $6.2 million between July 1 and Sept. 23, with $5.5 million coming from billionaire and ABC Supply founder Diane Hendricks, according to an RACC campaign financial report . Hendricks donated an additional $1.75 million to Senate races, according to the Committee to Elect a Republican Senate campaign financial report . While raising and spending money helps, it does not guarantee victory, according to Wisconsin Democracy Campaign Communications and Digital Director Molly Carmichael. “There’s no definitive answer on how much that money moves people,” Carmichael said. The RACC spent $14.3 million in the same July-Sept. period, allocating most of it to media buys and mailers for GOP incumbents and candidates, according to Wisconsin Public Radio . The Assembly Democratic Campaign Committee raised $6 million over the same period, with its largest donor giving $1 million, according to WPR. The committee spent $3 million overall, sending $375,000 to the Democratic Party of Wisconsin’s main account, according to WPR. Notable differences in strategy appear in the State Senate, which is currently controlled by an 18-15 Republican majority, according to WPR. CERS spent $2.7 million on media buys in three key races to save the party’s majority, while the State Senate Democratic Committee focused on backing State Rep. Jenna Jacobson, D-Oregon, who is running against incumbent Sen. Howard Marklein, R-Spring Green, for the Senate’s 17th District, sending $1.6 million in support, according to WPR. The governor’s race shows even wider gaps in spending, with Republicans spending $117.5 million and Democrats spending $48.7 million, according to WisPolitics . Republican nominee U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany, R-Wis., spent $47 million alone, while $48.7 million from Democrats includes Democratic nominee and Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley’s campaign, those who ran against him in the primary and outside groups, according to WisPolitics. Tiffany has received nearly $50 million in campaign funding, while Crowley has received almost $27 million. However, in the July 1 to Oct. 19 period, Crowley outraised Tiffany, receiving about $15.5 million, while Tiffany received just over $10 million. The pattern is not new, and spending has consistently risen since the 2010 Citizens United v. FEC ruling, which opened the door to more outside spending, according to Carmichael. The Citizens United ruling allowed corporations and labor unions to spend unlimited amounts independently to support or oppose political candidates, while leaving restrictions on direct contributions to candidates in place, according to the Federal Election Commission . “It all continues to trend upward, so … it’s not good, but it’s not surprising, and it continues to rise as we get into the future, and there has been some pretty stark jumps, especially in the gubernatorial election,” Carmichael said. Still, greater spending does not always mean a win, according to University of Wisconsin Political Science Professor David Canon . Campaign spending can increase candidates’ visibility through digital campaigns and mailers, but the effects vary depending on the race and the candidates involved, Canon said. “It’s actually a more interesting question than you’d think, because the intuitive answer is ‘well, of course money matters,'” Canon said. “If you have more money, it is better than having less money. And to a large extent, that’s true, but there’s an interesting wrinkle on it that the earliest research on this showed the opposite.” In the past, challengers have outspent incumbents and lost, while others have won spending far less, so challengers need enough money to be competitive, but spending beyond that threshold matters less, according to Canon. Where the money comes from can also hurt a campaign, as court rulings have lifted limits on what individuals can give to parties and what parties can spend directly on candidates, according to Canon. “Even with Tiffany having a fairly large financial edge right now, the fact that it came from just a handful of billionaires has become an issue that could backfire,” Canon said. Tiffany received 90% of his campaign contributions from three billionaires — Hendricks, Richard Uihlein and Elizabeth Uihlein — during the July to September reporting period, according to the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel. The larger trend is the increasing role of national money, as races once funded locally now draw heavily on out-of-state donors, which is part of nationalizing elections, according to Canon. Statewide candidates need money to spread their message, but grassroots campaigns have gained traction in Wisconsin and across the country with issues like data centers dominating conversations, according to Carmichael. “It is getting more and more expensive to run campaigns, and I think one thing that we’ve seen, in Wisconsin especially, but really in all competitive races around the country, is the increased importance of national money,” Canon said.

title: Zoo’s new leader started career at Shedd: ‘Fish were my first love’ - The Cap Times
text: The Cap Times is an independent newsroom serving Madison and Wisconsin. Sign up for the Morning Update to receive news in your inbox each morning. The Henry Vilas Zoo is welcoming a new director after nearly seven months of interim leadership. Jeff Mitchell assumed the role Oct. 19, bringing experience from zoos and aquariums across North America, including Chicago’s Shedd Aquarium and Brookfield Zoo. Most recently, he led the Saskatoon Forestry Farm Park and Zoo in Saskatchewan, Canada. “Madison is like Saskatoon. It's a big, small town,” Mitchell said. “I'm really excited to be able to be a part of this community.” Mitchell succeeds Ronda Schwetz, who retired after 15 years as director. Janine Wachter has served as interim director for most of this year and will return to her role as deputy director at the Alliant Energy Center. The Cap Times spoke with Mitchell about his career, what drew him to Madison and what he envisions for the zoo. The following has been edited for clarity and brevity. I'm curious what attracted you to Henry Vilas Zoo and what led you to making the decision to accept the role. There's a couple things that really attracted me to come here, and the first one is very, very personal. Growing up, my family and I always went to Lincoln Park Zoo, which is the free zoo in Chicago. It wasn't until I was older that I realized the importance of a free zoo and how much we can be a real integral part of the community. This is my first opportunity to really work for a completely free facility like we are here. Kids can have the same experiences I did growing up, and now I get to be a part of that. That's just an amazing feeling. The staff here is amazing, and man, they are just excited and dedicated, and really looking out for the best interests of the animals and animal welfare. So it was just kind of the perfect opportunity for me. Madison is such a cool town, and it's a really loving community. I was excited about that. You began your zoo career at Shedd Aquarium. How did you get into working with zoos, and what led you to Shedd? Well, I've always been a fish person. Fish were my first love. A lot of people find that weird. I've always loved the chemistry and the filtration and the intricacies of taking care of fish. When you're taking care of fish, you have to worry about the pH of the water and the oxygen they breathe, but when you take care of a mammal, you don't have to worry about how much oxygen is in the air. I’ve always just been fascinated by that. Jeff Mitchell, Henry Vilas Zoo's new director, began his zoo career decades ago at Shedd Aquarium in Chicago. When I started, I promised myself I would never get into management. I never wanted to. But after 11 years, I was like, I think I could do a little better job. The first four places I applied all said I had great animal experience, but no management experience. So, I took a gamble and left the field and became a project manager. I managed about $250 million worth of construction projects for three years. I could then come back into the field and say: “Look, I can do this. I'm capable of doing these things.” I bounced around a bit afterward … and for the last six and a half years I've been up in Saskatchewan, Canada. What are you most proud of from your work in Canada? The biggest thing is probably developing an animal welfare program and developing a training and enrichment program up there. There wasn't a great program. Being able to help the staff realize what they could do and help them grow and really take ownership of their work were some of the best things that I did. I take a lot of pride in being able to do that. I really encourage the open, honest and sometimes brutal conversations you have to have. I want the staff comfortable enough to tell me when I screw up. I am a person, and I'm going to make mistakes. I've been in the zoo field for 35 years, but that doesn't mean I have a clue for some things. And so I rely on our staff's expertise and knowledge to really help me help them move forward. We did some other things that were phenomenal. We added a butterfly exhibit, which was extremely popular. We updated quite a few other exhibits. But ultimately I'm most proud of all the work the staff did, and that I got to help them do. Do you have any goals for the zoo within your first year or five years? My first couple months are going to be really focused on getting to know the staff and what's going on here. I started shadowing today (Oct. 27), which is always always fun. I'm shadowing the zookeepers, our maintenance people and a lot of different people to get to know the areas and what's working, what's not working, and what we can do to help make things better. County Executive (Melissa) Agard told me during the interview process that she wants the zoo to be fossil fuel-free by 2040, and so that's a really crazy goal that I'm excited to be able to work on with our conservation and maintenance staff. We put up a new solar pavilion, and we're looking at potentially putting up some more. We're looking at different ways we can convert some of our buildings to all-electric so we can then supply the electricity through solar. The Henry Vilas Zoo just celebrated 50 years of AZA (Association of Zoos and Aquariums) accreditation, which is amazing. And I just want to continue the tradition that the people for the last 50 years have done. And, man, I just want to be a tiny little part of the history of Henry Vilas Zoo, and I'll be able to retire as a happy person in 15 years. What misconception, if any, about zoos do you wish more people understood? What I don't think a lot of people really understand is when we're doing breeding programs, we're not just breeding animals because we want to breed them. We work with zoos all over North America, all AZA zoos, and we actually have procedures … that tells us who to breed with whom, when and how. If you were to look at all the orangutans in North American zoos, we can go back multiple generations and tell you how everyone is related to everyone. It's really not just a willy-nilly, picking it out of a hat. It's really scientific. A lot of these animals are extremely endangered in the wild, or actually starting to go extinct in the wild. At some point, orangutans aren't going to be in the wild anymore, and the only population that will be left is in zoos. And if we ever want a chance to be able to bring them back out, we need to have those populations. Some of the other things that a lot of facilities are doing now is … biobanks, where they take samples of blood, muscle or tissues from animals, and then they freeze them at minus 160 degrees Celsius so they can keep these tissues. And then what happens is you can pull that tissue out and start to grow it again after it's been at minus 160, and so you can do research on it, or extract DNA from it. Biobanking has become huge, and it's one of the ways that we can save DNA and tissues from animals that are alive today. Who knows what we're going to be able to develop in science in the next 20 or 30 years that might help bring back some of those species? It's really cool, and it's really on the cutting edge. And those are some of the neat things that we get to do as zoos. Is that happening at the Henry Vilas Zoo, or is it something that you're hoping to implement at some point? I'm not exactly sure if we've started biobanking here in North America. We started doing it with some of the facilities up there in Canada. So I'm guessing we'll be doing something like that here, if we're not doing something like that already.

The larger trend is the increasing role of national money, as races once funded locally now draw heavily on out-of-state donors, which is part of nationalizing elections, according to Canon. Statewide candidates need money to spread their message, but grassroots campaigns have gained traction in Wisconsin and across the country with issues like data centers dominating conversations, according to Carmichael. “It is getting more and more expensive to run campaigns, and I think one thing that we’ve seen, in Wisconsin especially, but really in all competitive races around the country, is the increased importance of national money,” Canon said.

title: 6 key questions Madison planners face about regulating data centers - The Cap Times
text: The Cap Times is an independent newsroom serving Madison and Wisconsin. Sign up for the Morning Update to receive news in your inbox each morning. With Madison’s one-year moratorium on data center construction set to expire in January, Madison residents pressed city staff this week on draft regulations aimed at restricting so-called “hyperscale” facilities. The proposed framework would divide allowed data centers into three categories: buildings under 10,000 square feet, or about twice the size of a fast food restaurant; buildings up to 50,000 square feet, or about the size of an average bowling alley; and buildings up to 100,000 square feet, or around the size of a grocery or department store. Data centers over 100,000 square feet would be banned. Potential locations for new data centers — facilities that house computer or network equipment used for storing, managing, processing and transmitting digital data — would be narrowed down as the size of a building increases. Smaller data centers, which are often tenants or sub-uses within larger facilities, would be permitted in a variety of nonresidential zones, including mixed-use, downtown, industrial, employment and “campus institutional” districts like the University of Wisconsin-Madison. Mid-sized data centers would be allowed in most employment and industrial zonings, along with campus-institutional districts. Larger data centers would be restricted to industrial areas. Other regulations would also increase with size, with fewer restrictions on smaller data centers. One potential limit would see smaller data centers banned on the ground floor in certain areas where planners prefer more public uses, for example. “If we're going to potentially allow data centers downtown — (where) there are already some in existence — we want to be preserving the ground floor for active uses like shops and bars and things that are creating that kind of vibrant downtown,” city planner Lisa Ernest said. The Cap Times welcomes tips from readers to help us inform our community. Email tips@captimes.com or visit captimes.com/tips for more options. Noise mitigation plans would be instituted only for mid-sized and larger facilities, with required inspection by a sound engineer. The proposal would set up 1,000-foot buffer zones between mid-sized and larger data centers to avoid creating “data center campuses” in certain areas of town. Larger data centers would need to be built at least 300 feet from residential buildings to reduce impacts like noise. Mid- and larger-sized data centers would be prohibited in areas planned for transit-intensive development. Regulation of data centers has drawn interest in and around Madison. Dane County and Sun Prairie also have moratoriums on new construction, and fierce public debate followed a proposed data center in DeForest . At Madison’s virtual meeting Oct. 27 about data center regulations, the number of residents registered for the meeting exceeded its allowed capacity. Residents asked around 70 questions, many of which fell into six broader themes. City leaders said the draft regulations are meant to strike a balance between the needs of local businesses and public concern over the potential impacts of so-called “hyperscale” data centers, like Meta’s $1 billion project in Beaver Dam . “We're trying to move through this moratorium to come up with the rules that aim to restrict all types and sizes of data centers in the city, while meeting the data needs of local entities like hospitals and research centers,” Deputy Mayor Christie Baumel said. City staff noted at least six standalone data centers exist in Madison, ranging from 1,200 to 17,000 square feet. Those data centers have not caused issues for the city or produced public complaints, Planning Director Meagan Tuttle said. “We have had smaller data centers operating in the city without many people even knowing that they were there,” Tuttle said. “We anticipate that we could adopt rules that would allow for those types of facilities to continue to operate in the city successfully.” A complete ban on data centers could land the city in legal hot water, Tuttle added. “We do have to be mindful of our requirements and limitations of using zoning to discriminate against certain types of businesses under state law and under Wisconsin case law,” she said. “While we can allow or disallow different types of businesses in our community, we have to be careful not to single out a specific type of business when the way that it operates isn't significantly different from other types of businesses or uses in our community already.” For the same reason, the city cannot extend its 12-month moratorium to give others like state lawmakers time to develop regulations, Tuttle added. Local governments are limited under state law in their ability to regulate water or energy usage. For instance, cities must allow users to connect to the municipal water system and cannot restrict the flow of water to facilities. The state Public Service Commission regulates energy providers in Wisconsin. But regulating the size of data centers could be an indirect vehicle for limiting potential strain on infrastructure, as well as other concerns like noise, city officials said. Data centers under 40,000 square feet generally require 500 kilowatts to 3 megawatts of electricity, or enough to power around 500 to 2,900 houses. The largest facilities can require nearly 2 gigawatts of electricity, or roughly equal to the power requirements of 100,000 homes. “Size alone, which is one of the main things that's within our purview to regulate, is a proxy,” Tuttle said at a Plan Commission meeting on data centers last month. City planners said they drew from research on other places in Wisconsin and across the country for the proposed upper limit. Data centers under that size are generally less likely to support demand for artificial intelligence. The size is also in the “lower end” of spatial and infrastructure demands among larger facilities, city staff said, though one resident noted Milwaukee has proposed a 60,000-square-foot limit. That size stands in stark contrast to the 2.5 million-square-foot data center currently under construction in Port Washington , designed to support OpenAI and Oracle. “The building does have to be a certain size to support the kind of AI modeling, AI training and the amount of servers they need,” Ernest said. “So at 100,000 square feet, we really felt like we were shifting away from any kind of hyperscale AI data center kind of building.” In this December 2025 file photo, Laurie Frey attends a protest on the steps of the Wisconsin state Capitol building in opposition to proposed data centers in Wisconsin. City staff pointed to 300-foot ordinances in cities in northern Virginia’s “ data center alley ,” which allow for similar size facilities as Madison is proposing. Size restrictions, they said, would limit noise from mechanical equipment like generators, which can only be used as backup sources of energy. Mid-sized data centers are unlikely to generate enough noise to require a buffer, Ernest said. “We tried to look to real world examples and what other communities are doing when establishing that buffer,” she said. “A 50,000-square-foot data center, from our understanding and looking at other uses in industrial areas, are not in our mind significantly different from other industrial uses in the city.” One resident asked whether the city would ban data centers from being near schools and daycare centers. Many schools, city staff said, are in residential areas and would be covered by the proposed 300-foot buffer. Daycare centers are allowed in residential, employment and industrial zones, making a space between these facilities and larger data centers more difficult to implement and enforce. “The focus is on putting daycares where people live, so if we're buffering from residential districts, that will include the daycare centers that are there,” Ernest said. “The administration of buffering from specific uses is something that we're still looking into, but it is difficult to manage and understand where these uses are and are not over time.” Madison’s noise ordinance is designed around sounds that humans can hear and does not include very high or very low frequencies. Industrial facilities already cannot emit noise that would be measured above 65 A-weighted decibels in neighboring residential properties. Some residents raised concerns about the effects of low frequency noise and vibrations from data centers. Low frequencies are measured in C-weighted decibels, which aren’t included in the noise ordinance. Ernest said the city is aware of those concerns. Baumel said the city is contemplating amendments to its noise ordinance in light of the discussion of data centers to include measures of low frequency noise. Madison's industrial areas, shaded in orange, would allow for large data centers, though this map does not account for a 300-foot buffer between such facilities and residential areas. City staff said there are no active proposals to build data centers, nor are they aware of plans for specific sites. At last month’s Plan Commission meeting, city staff showed a map of industrial zones where large data centers could be constructed, with most of the potential sites on the east side, along with several areas on the south side and smaller sites on the west side. That map did not account for a 300-foot buffer zone between data centers and industrial areas, Tuttle said. “We have not identified the locations where we prefer that data centers be located,” she said. Proposed regulations of new data centers are expected for initial discussion at the city’s Plan Commission in late November, with hearings by the Business and Economic Resources Committee and the Sustainable Madison Committee in December. The Plan Commission would then review recommendations a second time in January. The full City Council would need to vote on any ordinance changes before the moratorium expires Jan. 24.

title: Wisconsin voters face 3 proposed constitutional amendments on the ballot - WKOW
text: Wisconsin voters face 3 proposed constitutional amendments on the ballot MADISON (WKOW) — Wisconsin voters will decide on three constitutional amendments on the ballot that cover prohibiting governor veto power, prohibiting closures on places of worship and prohibiting governmental entity discrimination. The first constitutional amendment question asks, "Shall section 10 (1) (c) of article V of the constitution be amended to prohibit the governor, in exercising his or her partial veto authority, from creating or increasing or authorizing the creation or increase of any tax or fee?" A "yes" vote would amend the Wisconsin Constitution and put limitations on the governor's partial veto power relating to creating or increasing any tax or fee. A "no" vote opposes amending the Wisconsin Constitution and would leave the governor's partial veto power as it is. This proposed constitutional amendment would stop governors from using their partial veto authority to authorize or create an increase of a tax or fee, according to Sterling Knoche with the State Democracy Research Initiative. It would not prevent a governor from using the partial veto power to decrease a tax or fee. The amendment comes in response to Gov. Tony Evers using his partial veto power in what became known as the 400-year veto . If the amendment passes, it would not undo that veto but would prevent similar uses of that power in the future. Knoche said this amendment differs from past changes because it focuses on the purpose of the veto rather than just the form it can take. It would limit a tool in the governor's toolbox, but only in specific instances related to taxes and fees. On October 21st, Republican candidate Tom Tiffany and Democrat candidate David Crowley debated on various topics, including the 400-year veto. "I will never do a veto, like was done, to have a 400-year property tax increase. The veto authority should not be used to increase taxes," Tiffany said. "So we're going to end the 400-year property tax increase, and then we're going to take that additional 15 billion dollars that was in the last state budget, and we're going to use that to help fund our schools as other as well as other local units of government." According to the Wisconsin Watch , David Crowley said, "he would “absolutely not” vote for the governor’s veto amendment." The State Democracy Research Initiative at UW Madison Law has a full explainer here . State of Wisconsin Freedom to Gather in Places of Worship During an Emergency Referendum - QUESTION 2 The second constitutional amendment question asks, "Shall section 18 of article I of the constitution, which deals with religious liberty, be amended to prohibit the state or a political subdivision of the state from ordering the closure of, or forbidding gatherings in, places of worship in response to a state of emergency, including a public health emergency?" A "yes" vote would amend the Wisconsin Constitution and prevent state and local governments from closing and forbidding gatherings at places of worship . A "no" vote opposes amending the Wisconsin Constitution. Knoche explained that supporters would argue that during an emergency is when people feel they need to practice their religion most. "They feel it's such a fundamental right that it should never have the ability to forbid or close," Knoche said. The amendment's language leaves key terms undefined, including what constitutes a "place of worship" and what "forbid or closure" means. Questions remain about whether capacity restrictions would still be allowed. Opponents argue that existing law already offers strong religious freedom protections. "...during COVID the U.S. Supreme Court interpreted our freedom of religion clause to prevent unreasonable closures and restrictions on places of worship... our Supreme Court, in a different case, has said that our freedom of religion clause is even more protective than the federal one. So, putting those two together...the government already cannot close places of worship unless they have a really, really good reason," Knoche explained. The State Democracy Research Initiative at UW Madison Law has a full explainer here . State of Wisconsin Governmental Entity Discrimination Prohibited Referendum - QUESTION 3 The third constitutional amendment question asks, "Shall section 27 of article I of the constitution be created to prohibit governmental entities in the state from discriminating against, or granting preferential treatment to, any individual or group on the basis of race, sex, color, ethnicity, or national origin in public employment, public education, public contracting, or public administration?" A "yes" vote would amend the Wisconsin Constitution and support banning any governmental entity from discriminating or granting preferential treatment on the basis of the characteristics listed above. A "no" vote opposes amending the Wisconsin Constitution. Knoche explained that proponents of this amendment have referred to it as a 'DEI' amendment, saying "... it's unclear how that would work. These other amendments that have been on the books now for 20 plus years haven't been interpreted that way." For the first time, Wisconsin's constitution would explicitly prohibit discrimination based on these specific classes. "...that's a whole other flip side that isn't really being discussed," Knoche said. "We have a broad equal protection clause that doesn't allow you to discriminate already, but this would actually say you cannot discriminate based on these specific classes." Key terms like "preferential treatment" and "discrimination" are not defined in the measure, leaving questions about how it would be interpreted in court. The State Democracy Research Initiative at UW Madison Law has a full explainer here . You can see what will be on your ballot by heading to MyVote.WI.gov.
